claims.text: Under typical wear conditions, high-entropy-alloy protective coatings develop a self-generated nanoscale surface oxide layer.
The nanoscale oxide layer significantly enhances wear resistance by acting as a barrier against mechanical abrasion.
The as-deposited coatings have a homogeneous, metastable microstructure.
The coatings contain a balanced mixture of oxidation-active and inert elements.
A low, controlled oxygen content promotes surface oxidation during wear.
An inert atmosphere inhibits oxide formation during wear.
Mechanical load and temperature will be held comparable while ambient oxygen concentration is varied.
The oxide generated during wear is nanoscale and stable.
Reactive alloying elements such as Cr and Al oxidize during abrasive contact.
Oxidation of reactive alloying elements forms a thin, adherent oxide film.
The oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide film mitigates plastic deformation or microfracture.
Reduced direct contact and damage lead to lower wear rates.
Coatings tested in a slightly oxidizing atmosphere will exhibit a detectable oxide layer and lower wear rates than identical coatings tested in an inert atmosphere.
The predicted oxide-mediated reduction in wear should hold over the typical stress range of wear-resistant protective applications.
Coatings tested in an inert atmosphere, or coatings lacking sufficient oxidation-active elements, exhibit minimal oxide-layer formation.
A threshold level of oxidation-sensitive elements is required for a significant protective effect.
At very high loads, mechanical forces may overwhelm oxide formation or retention and diminish the protective effect.
No statistically significant wear-rate difference between oxidizing and inert conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of a correlation between oxide presence or thickness and improved wear performance would falsify the hypothesis.
